lesson.title: Many Genes, Many Cell Types: Gene Regulation in Eukaryotes
lesson.summary: Eukaryotic cells regulate gene expression through the same basic transcriptional logic as bacteria, but layer on chromatin packaging, enhancers acting at a distance, and combinations of transcription factors to let one genome produce many distinct cell types.
lesson.body:
The same basic problem prokaryotic cells solve with operons, making only the proteins that are currently needed, is even more demanding for eukaryotic cells. A multicellular eukaryote's cells all carry the same genome, yet a muscle cell, a neuron, and a skin cell each express strikingly different sets of genes to become and remain such different kinds of cells. Eukaryotic gene regulation has to be able to specify not just when a gene is on, but in which cell type, and often at which stage of development, it should be on. Eukaryotic genes are also, in contrast to bacterial operons, typically not grouped together under one shared promoter; each gene usually has its own promoter and is transcribed into its own separate mRNA, so coordinating many genes at once requires a different strategy than the shared operator of an operon.

The first additional layer of control in eukaryotic cells comes from chromatin structure. Eukaryotic DNA is wrapped around histone proteins to form nucleosomes and packaged further into chromatin, and how tightly that chromatin is packed at a given gene strongly affects whether the transcription machinery can even reach it. Tightly condensed chromatin, called heterochromatin, is largely inaccessible, and genes within it are effectively silenced. Loosely packed chromatin, called euchromatin, is far more accessible to RNA polymerase and the proteins that help recruit it. Cells adjust this packing through chemical modifications, collectively called epigenetic modifications because they change gene expression without altering the DNA sequence itself: methyl groups added to DNA, typically at cytosines, are generally associated with silencing a gene, while chemical modifications to the histone proteins, such as histone acetylation, tend to loosen chromatin and favor transcription. These marks can be maintained through cell division, which is part of how a cell's identity, once established, tends to be stably passed on to its daughter cells.

The second additional layer involves regulatory DNA sequences that can act from far away. Beyond the promoter itself, eukaryotic genes are commonly controlled by enhancers, which increase transcription, and silencers, which decrease it, either of which can sit thousands of base pairs upstream or downstream of the gene they regulate, or even within one of its introns. These distant elements work because the DNA between them and the promoter can loop around, bringing regulatory proteins bound at the enhancer into direct physical contact with the transcription machinery assembled at the promoter. The proteins that bind these sequences, transcription factors, are covered in detail in the next chapter.

The combination of many possible enhancers, many possible transcription factors, and variable chromatin accessibility gives eukaryotic cells an enormous amount of combinatorial control. A single gene's expression can depend on which particular set of transcription factors happens to be present and active in a given cell, since different cell types express different combinations of these regulatory proteins even though they all carry an identical genome. That combinatorial logic, rather than any single all or nothing switch, is largely how one genome gives rise to hundreds of distinct cell types over the course of development. Finally, it is worth noting that transcription is not the only level at which eukaryotic gene expression is controlled; regulation can also occur after an mRNA is made and after a protein is made, but transcriptional control, precisely because it prevents an unneeded mRNA from ever being made in the first place, remains the most efficient and heavily used level of control, in eukaryotic cells just as it is in bacteria.
